synopsis: The regulatory values are not directly comparable: UN R152 specifies commanded braking demand, ISO 3450 derives mean deceleration from stopping distance, MSHA assumes constant deceleration with separate response times, and New South Wales uses net deceleration on grade; pooled values therefore require conversion to a common definition [f13640, f13641]. NSW guidance proposes service/secondary-brake minima of 0.60/0.30 m/s² in service and 0.75/0.40 m/s² in type testing, with grade and mass corrections—not an adopted rule—whereas MSHA Table M-1 uses approximately 2.94 m/s² and MOSH emergency-stop targets are 1.9 m/s² above 20 km/h and 1.0 m/s² otherwise [f13946, f5989, f5560]. On-road requirements include braking demands of at least 5.0 m/s² under UN R152 and 4 m/s² under UN R131; the November 2024 FMVSS 127 amendment instead addresses false activation relative to manual braking, using a 0.25 g peak-deceleration threshold [f5993, f2520, f2617]. Although the synthesis says no universal maximum automatic deceleration exists, the more qualified finding is that no published universal safe maximum or tuned off-road deceleration values were found; South Africa Regulation 8.10 also prescribes no deceleration curve [f151, f13769, f5916, f2442]. The recommended approach is machine-family-specific limits: command the minimum of collision-avoidance need, traction, stability, brake capability and load limits, with a jerk limit, and derive stability caps through layered models and physical tests involving steering or articulation, cross-slope and relevant payloads [f11888, f152, f13840, f13770].
